statement: Because of netting, overall credit exposure in the OTC derivatives market grows at a lower rate than the notional growth of the market itself.
explanation: Close-out netting makes exposures non-additive, so credit exposure scales more slowly than notional. This is why the size and liquidity of the OTC derivatives market can grow without counterparty risk becoming unmanageable.
originalText: Netting means overall credit exposure in the market grows at a lower rate than the notional growth of the market itself.

statement: Because of netting, overall credit exposure in the OTC derivatives market grows at a higher rate than the notional growth of the market.
explanation: Netting can only reduce or leave unchanged the exposure, so it cannot make exposure grow faster than notional. Exposure grows at a lower rate than notional.
originalText: Netting means overall credit exposure in the market grows at a higher rate than the notional growth of the market.
correction: Because of netting, overall credit exposure in the OTC derivatives market grows at a lower rate than the notional growth of the market.

statement: Because of netting, overall credit exposure in the OTC derivatives market grows at the same rate as the notional growth of the market.
explanation: If exposure grew at the same rate as notional, netting would give no benefit. Netting reduces exposure relative to notional, so exposure grows more slowly.
originalText: Netting means overall credit exposure grows at the same rate as the notional growth of the market.
correction: Because of netting, overall credit exposure in the OTC derivatives market grows at a lower rate than the notional growth of the market.

statement: Netting eliminates all counterparty credit exposure, so market size is no longer limited by credit risk.
explanation: Netting reduces counterparty exposure but does not eliminate it, because a positive net amount can remain after offsetting trade values.

statement: Futures are more beneficial for netting than options bought with up-front premiums, because a futures position can have a negative mark-to-market value that offsets positive exposures.
explanation: Netting only helps when negative MtM values can offset positive ones. Futures can move to negative MtM, whereas an option bought with an up-front premium never has negative MtM for the holder.
originalText: Futures.

statement: Options with up-front premiums have a more beneficial effect on netting than futures do.
explanation: A bought option with an up-front premium has non-negative MtM for the holder, so it has nothing to offset other positive exposures. Futures can have negative MtM and therefore help netting more.
originalText: Options with up‑front premiums.
correction: Futures have a more beneficial effect on netting than options with up-front premiums do.

changes.to: than options with up-front premiums do

statement: OTC uncollateralized derivatives typically carry no routine collateral requirement, so participants do not normally post collateral.
explanation: Uncollateralized trading means no CSA or margining arrangement covers the trades, so the party with positive MtM bears the full counterparty exposure with no routine collateral flows.
originalText: There is no routine collateral requirement; participants do not typically post collateral in these transactions.

statement: For OTC uncollateralized derivatives, participants are typically required to post collateral based on credit ratings at predetermined intervals.
explanation: Posting collateral according to ratings describes a rating-triggered CSA, which is a collateralized arrangement. Uncollateralized OTC derivatives have no routine collateral requirement.
originalText: Participants are required to post collateral based on credit ratings at predetermined intervals.

statement: For OTC uncollateralized derivatives, collateral is pooled among all participants to cover the obligations within the entire market segment.
explanation: Pooled, mutualized resources describe a CCP default fund. Bilateral uncollateralized OTC trades have no market-wide collateral pool and no routine collateral at all.
originalText: Collateral is pooled among all participants to cover the obligations within the entire market segment.

statement: For OTC uncollateralized derivatives, a one-time collateral is posted at the start of the contract and released upon successful settlement.
explanation: An upfront amount held until settlement is itself collateral (an initial margin or independent amount). Uncollateralized derivatives have no routine collateral requirement.
originalText: A one‑time collateral is posted at the start of the contract and released upon successful settlement.

statement: If two counterparties follow best practices under a bilateral collateral agreement, collateral posting should be continuous for both of them.
explanation: Margin is not posted continuously because that would be operationally costly. Calls occur at agreed frequencies and in blocks.
originalText: If they followed best practices, collateral posting should be continuous for both of them.

statement: As a counterparty risk mitigant, collateral posting is generally superior to a reset feature.
explanation: A reset is essentially a periodic, infrequent settlement, which makes it a weaker form of margining. Collateral posting is therefore generally the stronger mitigant.

statement: Variation margin is a type of collateral that aims to track the change in valuation (the change in MtM) of the position over time.
explanation: Variation margin follows changes in the MtM of the position, whereas initial margin is set independently of current exposure.

statement: Under a bilateral collateral agreement, a party with positive MtM calls for collateral and a party with negative MtM is required to post collateral itself.
explanation: This is how two-way (bilateral) collateral works: whichever party is out of the money posts and whichever is in the money receives.
originalText: As a bilateral agreement, in the case of a positive MtM the party will call for collateral, and in the case of a negative MtM the party will be required to post collateral itself.

statement: Collateralization reduces market, operational and liquidity risk.
explanation: Collateral reduces counterparty credit risk, but it introduces market risk (collateral value changes), operational risk (legal and processing issues) and liquidity risk (funding and selling collateral).
originalText: Reduces market, operational, and liquidity risk.

statement: Collateralization reduces regulatory capital requirements.
explanation: Collateral lowers counterparty exposure and therefore the capital required against it, which is one motivation for collateral management.
originalText: Reduces capital requirements.

statement: Collateralization allows more competitive pricing of counterparty risk.
explanation: Because secured exposure is smaller, counterparty risk can be priced more tightly, which is one motivation for collateral management.
originalText: Allows for more competitive pricing of counterparty risk.

statement: Collateralization reduces credit exposure.
explanation: Collateral directly offsets positive MtM exposure, which is the primary benefit of collateralization.
originalText: Reduces credit exposure.

statement: A valuation agent calculates the threshold.
explanation: The threshold is negotiated and written into the CSA at inception. The valuation agent applies it but does not calculate it.
originalText: To calculate the threshold

statement: A typical calculation performed by a valuation agent is credit exposure including the impact of netting.
explanation: The valuation agent works out current exposure net of netting as part of the margin calculation.
originalText: To calculate credit exposure including the impact of netting

statement: A typical calculation performed by a valuation agent is the uncollateralized exposure.
explanation: Total uncollateralized exposure, after posted collateral and haircuts, is one of the valuation agent's standard margin calculations.
originalText: To calculate the uncollateralized exposure

statement: A typical calculation performed by a valuation agent is the delivery or return amount, which is the amount of collateral to be posted by either counterparty.
explanation: The delivery or return (credit support) amount is the main output of the valuation agent's margin calculation.
originalText: To calculate the delivery or return amount (the amount of collateral to be posted by either counterparty)

statement: If both counterparties to a credit support annex are named valuation agent, each calls for collateral when it has positive exposure, which can lead to disputes and delays, and appointing a third-party valuation agent is a common remedy.
explanation: Two independent sets of calculations can disagree, creating dispute and delay risk. A third-party valuation agent can resolve disputes, process substitutions and produce daily valuation reports.
originalText: Each bank calls for collateral when it has positive exposure, which can lead to disputes and delays; appointing a third‑party valuation agent is a common remedy.

statement: A collateral policy that prioritizes liquidity and freedom from price uncertainty relies mainly on cash, supplemented by high-quality government securities.
explanation: Cash has no price variability and is the most common collateral, while government securities are liquid and low risk. Other collateral types carry more price uncertainty or liquidity problems.
originalText: Rely mainly on cash, supplemented by high‑quality government securities.

statement: Under title transfer, legal ownership of the margin passes to the receiver (possibly with usage restrictions), whereas under a security interest the giver retains ownership and the receiver holds a claim exercisable on default.
explanation: A security interest (a pledge, typical of New York law) leaves ownership with the giver. Title transfer (typical of English law) passes ownership outright.
originalText: Under title transfer, legal ownership of the margin passes to the receiver (possibly with usage restrictions); under a security interest the giver retains ownership and the receiver holds a claim exercisable on default.

statement: Under a security interest, legal ownership of the margin passes to the receiver, whereas under title transfer it stays with the giver.
explanation: The two arrangements are reversed in this statement. Title transfer passes legal ownership to the receiver, while a security interest leaves it with the giver.
originalText: Under a security interest, legal ownership of the margin passes to the receiver; under title transfer it stays with the giver.
correction: Under title transfer, legal ownership of the margin passes to the receiver, whereas under a security interest it stays with the giver.

statement: Under a security interest, the receiver of margin may freely use the margin assets, whereas under title transfer it may not.
explanation: This reverses who has freedom of use. The receiver of title-transferred assets can generally use them freely, while under a security interest the giver still owns them.
originalText: Under a security interest, the receiver may freely use the margin assets; under title transfer it may not.
correction: Under title transfer, the receiver of margin may freely use the margin assets, whereas under a security interest it may not.

changes.from: Under a security interest, the receiver

statement: Under title transfer, the giver keeps the margin assets and is protected if the receiver defaults, whereas under a security interest the giver is an unsecured creditor.
explanation: This reverses the giver's protection. Under title transfer the giver is an unsecured creditor of the receiver for return of the assets, so a security interest is preferable for the giver.
originalText: Under title transfer, the giver keeps the margin assets and is protected if the receiver defaults; under a security interest it is an unsecured creditor.

statement: Cash is the most common collateral but can become scarce in stress, while noncash collateral can introduce rehypothecation issues and price uncertainty.
explanation: Cash is the most widely used collateral, but its supply can dry up in stress. Noncash collateral may be preferred for liquidity but brings rehypothecation problems and price uncertainty.

statement: Government agency securities are free of price uncertainty, which is why they are always preferred over cash and no issues arise from their reuse.
explanation: Agency securities carry price uncertainty and rehypothecation issues, and cash is the most common type of collateral.

statement: Letters of credit and equities are the most common collateral because they are the easiest to value and to rehypothecate.
explanation: Cash is the most common collateral. Letters of credit and equities are less common and are not the easiest assets to value.

statement: Noncash collateral eliminates the need for daily marking to market because its value cannot change between collateral calls.
explanation: Noncash collateral is valued by marking to market, typically daily, precisely because its value does change.

statement: A request to recover posted collateral is satisfied only if the counterparty posts an alternative amount of eligible collateral with equivalent value, after applying the relevant haircut.
explanation: A substitution is valid when the replacement is eligible collateral whose haircut-adjusted value equals that of the collateral released. Asset class and currency need not match.
originalText: posts an alternative amount of eligible collateral with equivalent value, after applying the relevant haircut.

statement: Under a standard collateral agreement, recovering posted securities requires the counterparty to post a replacement in exactly the same asset class as the collateral previously posted.
explanation: Substitution does not require the same asset class. Any eligible collateral of equivalent haircut-adjusted value works.
originalText: posts a replacement in exactly the same asset class as the collateral previously posted.

statement: Under a standard collateral agreement, recovering posted securities requires a valid replacement of equal value, and the haircut amount must be posted in cash.
explanation: The haircut is built into the amount of replacement collateral, so it does not have to be paid separately in cash.
originalText: posts a valid replacement of equal value to the collateral withdrawn, but must post the haircut amount in cash.

statement: Under a standard collateral agreement, recovering posted securities requires the counterparty to post a replacement in a different asset class from the collateral previously posted.
explanation: A different asset class is permitted but is not required. The condition is that the replacement is eligible and equal in haircut-adjusted value.
originalText: posts a replacement in a different asset class from the collateral previously posted.

statement: Collateral that need not be segregated and can be rehypothecated gives the receiver a funding benefit from reusing it, but if its value is positively related to the poster's credit quality it provides only limited counterparty risk mitigation.
explanation: Rehypothecation lets the receiver reuse the collateral, lowering funding cost. Collateral whose value falls as the poster's credit quality deteriorates loses value just when default is likely, so protection is only partial.
originalText: A funding benefit from reusing the collateral, but only limited counterparty risk mitigation because its value falls as Bank A’s credit quality deteriorates.

statement: Rehypothecable collateral gives its receiver a funding benefit only and no counterparty risk mitigation, because rehypothecable collateral is never available at default.
explanation: Collateral still reduces exposure to the poster. Rehypothecation reduces, but does not eliminate, the availability of the collateral at default.
originalText: A funding benefit only; it gives no counterparty risk mitigation because rehypothecable collateral is never available at default.

statement: Collateral received gives full counterparty risk mitigation, because posted collateral always offsets the exposure completely.
explanation: Collateral does not always offset exposure completely. For example, its value can fall with the poster's credit quality, so the mitigation is only partial.
originalText: Full counterparty risk mitigation and a funding benefit, because posted collateral always offsets the exposure completely.

statement: From a counterparty risk perspective, rehypothecating initial margin is riskier than rehypothecating variation margin, because initial margin is meant to be recoverable while variation margin can be set off against the amount owed.
explanation: If the receiver of reused initial margin defaults, the poster is left with an unsecured claim for its return. Variation margin reflects an amount currently owed, so it can be set off on default.
originalText: Rehypothecation of initial margin.

statement: If the goal is to minimize funding costs, both parties to a credit support annex prefer to avoid rehypothecation rights.
explanation: Rehypothecation reduces funding cost, so a party minimizing funding costs would seek rehypothecation rights rather than avoid them.
originalText: If the goal is to minimize funding costs, both parties prefer to avoid rehypothecation rights.

statement: For variation margin, both parties probably prefer rehypothecation rights and probably will not require segregation.
explanation: Variation margin is quasi-settlement of the amount owed, and set-off limits the counterparty risk of reusing it.
originalText: With respect to variation margin, both parties probably prefer rehypothecation rights and probably will not require segregation.

statement: For initial margin, both parties are likely to insist on non-rehypothecation and will probably require segregation.
explanation: Initial margin is an over-collateralization buffer that the poster expects back, so it needs to be segregated and not reused.
originalText: With respect to initial margin, both parties are likely to insist on non‑rehypothecation and will probably require segregation.

statement: Segregation protects the collateral poster against loss of the collateral on the receiver's default, but may raise funding costs because the collateral cannot be reused.
explanation: Segregation lowers counterparty risk for the poster but forgoes reuse of the collateral, which raises funding cost.
originalText: Segregation protects the collateral poster against loss of the collateral on the receiver’s default, but may raise funding costs because the collateral cannot be reused.

statement: If a party that rehypothecated collateral cannot get it back because the party it passed it to defaults, its obligation to return the collateral to the original poster is extinguished.
explanation: Rehypothecating collateral does not discharge the duty to return it to the poster. A downstream default therefore creates a double loss: the lost collateral and the continuing liability to return it.
originalText: If Counterparty A defaults and cannot return the rehypothecated collateral, the institution’s obligation to return collateral to Counterparty B is extinguished.

statement: If substituted collateral meets all eligibility criteria, a substitution request by the collateral poster cannot be refused by the receiver.
explanation: A substitution of equivalent value in eligible collateral cannot be refused.
originalText: If the substituted collateral meets all eligibility criteria, a substitution request by Counterparty B cannot be refused by the institution.

statement: If a party that rehypothecated collateral cannot recover it because the party it passed it to defaults, the rehypothecating party suffers a loss and still owes the collateral back to the original poster.
explanation: This is the two-fold risk of rehypothecation: the collateral is lost and the liability to return it remains.
originalText: If Counterparty A defaults and cannot return the rehypothecated collateral, the institution suffers a loss and still owes the collateral back to Counterparty B.

statement: Segregation works contrary to rehypothecation and may create funding problems when replacing collateral that could have been rehypothecated.
explanation: Segregated collateral cannot be reused, so the receiver must fund replacements for collateral that rehypothecation would otherwise have supplied.

statement: Under the uncleared margin requirements, variation margin must be exchanged regularly (for example, daily) with a zero threshold and a minimum transfer amount not exceeding EUR 500,000.
explanation: Variation margin is full margin with a zero threshold, an MTA of at most EUR 500,000, and applied in full from the start of the rules. It can be rehypothecated and netted.
originalText: Variation margin must be exchanged regularly (for example, daily) with a zero threshold and a minimum transfer amount not exceeding EUR 500,000.

statement: Under the uncleared margin requirements, variation margin may be subject to a threshold of up to EUR 50 million, provided the minimum transfer amount is zero.
explanation: The EUR 50 million threshold relates to initial margin. Variation margin has a zero threshold.
originalText: Variation margin may be subject to a threshold of up to EUR 50 million, provided the minimum transfer amount is zero.

statement: Under the uncleared margin requirements, variation margin requirements are phased in over six years according to aggregate notional, and the minimum transfer amount is unrestricted.
explanation: The multi-year phase-in by notional applies to initial margin. Variation margin applied in full from the start and its minimum transfer amount is capped at EUR 500,000.
originalText: Variation margin requirements are phased in over six years according to aggregate notional, and the minimum transfer amount is unrestricted.

statement: Under the uncleared margin requirements, variation margin must be segregated with a third-party custodian and cannot be rehypothecated or netted.
explanation: Segregation, no rehypothecation and no netting describe initial margin. Variation margin may be reused and netted.
originalText: Variation margin must be segregated with a third‑party custodian and cannot be rehypothecated or netted.

statement: Under the uncleared margin requirements, initial margin may be based on validated internal models or regulatory tables, using a 99%, 10-day move calibrated to a stress period.
explanation: Initial margin covers an extreme but plausible move at 99% confidence over 10 days, calibrated to historical data that includes a period of significant financial stress.
originalText: Initial margin may be based on validated internal models or regulatory tables, using a 99%, 10‑day move calibrated to a stress period.

statement: Under the uncleared margin requirements, initial margin must be calculated using the regulatory schedule only, because internal models are not permitted.
explanation: The rules allow either regulatory tables or validated internal models.
originalText: Initial margin must be calculated using the regulatory schedule only, because internal models are not permitted for initial margin.

statement: Under the uncleared margin requirements, initial margin should be calibrated to data from recent calm periods, because this reduces the procyclicality of margin over time.
explanation: The calibration data must include a period of significant financial stress, and it is this stress calibration that reduces procyclicality. Calm-period data would understate margin.
originalText: Initial margin should be calibrated to data from recent calm periods, because this reduces the procyclicality of margin over time.

statement: Under the uncleared margin requirements, initial margin applies in full to all new and existing trades of all covered entities from the start, exactly as variation margin did.
explanation: This confuses initial margin with variation margin. Initial margin was phased in through declining notional thresholds and need not be applied to existing contracts.
originalText: Initial margin applied in full to all new and existing trades of all covered entities from the start, exactly as variation margin did.

statement: A covered entity that collects initial margin on non-centrally-cleared derivatives must segregate it with a third-party custodian or under other legally binding arrangements, and must not rehypothecate, repledge or reuse it.
explanation: Segregation and no reuse ensure that posting initial margin does not itself raise counterparty risk, because the margin is protected if the collecting party defaults.
originalText: Bank B must segregate the margin with a third‑party custodian or under other legally binding arrangements, and must not rehypothecate, repledge or reuse it.

statement: Initial margin on non-centrally-cleared derivatives should be sized on a 95% confidence level over a five-day horizon using historical data from calm periods.
explanation: The standard is a 99% confidence level, a 10-day horizon and data that includes a period of financial stress.
originalText: Bank B should size the margin on a 95% confidence level over a five‑day horizon using historical data from calm periods.
correction: Initial margin on non-centrally-cleared derivatives should be sized on a 99% confidence level over a 10-day horizon using historical data from stress periods.

changes.from: 95% confidence level over a five-day horizon

statement: A covered entity may net the initial margin it collects against the initial margin it posts to its counterparty, and may reuse it as it would variation margin.
explanation: Initial margin is exchanged on a gross basis with no netting, and only variation margin may be reused.
originalText: Bank B may net the margin it collects against the margin it posts to Bank A, and may reuse it as it would variation margin.

statement: A covered entity may hold the initial margin it collects in its own accounts and rehypothecate it, since initial margin is simply additional margin.
explanation: Holding it in its own accounts and rehypothecating it contradicts the segregation and no-reuse requirements for initial margin.
originalText: Bank B may hold the margin in its own accounts and rehypothecate it, since initial margin is simply additional margin.

statement: A central counterparty serves as an intermediary, stepping in between the original trading parties to assume their rights.
explanation: Through novation the CCP becomes the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer, so the original counterparties no longer face each other's default risk directly.
originalText: A CCP serves as an intermediary, stepping in between the original trading parties to assume their rights.

statement: A central counterparty acts primarily as a regulatory body, setting legal and operational standards for the OTC derivatives market.
explanation: A CCP is a clearing entity that is itself subject to regulation. It is not the rule-setter for the market.
originalText: A CCP acts primarily as a regulatory body, setting legal and operational standards for the OTC derivatives market.

statement: A central counterparty functions as a financial advisor, providing guidance on risk management and investment strategies to parties in OTC derivatives.
explanation: A CCP gives no investment or risk advice. It manages its own risk through margin and default resources.
originalText: A CCP functions as a financial advisor, providing guidance on risk management and investment strategies to parties involved in OTC derivatives.

statement: A central counterparty operates as a market maker, ensuring liquidity and setting prices for OTC derivatives.
explanation: A CCP does not make markets or set prices. Trading and price formation occur between market participants, and the CCP clears the resulting trades.
originalText: A CCP operates as a market maker, ensuring liquidity and setting prices for OTC derivatives.

statement: The key challenges for central clearing of OTC derivative products are product complexity, illiquid products, the presence of wrong-way risk and lack of standardization.
explanation: A CCP needs standardized, liquid, non-exotic products without wrong-way risk so that it can value positions, set margin and close out defaulted positions. Many OTC products fail these tests.
originalText: Product complexity, illiquid products, presence of wrong‑way risk, and lack of standardization.

statement: A CCP has a matched book and bears no net market risk, but it takes on the counterparty risk of its clearing members, which is centralized in the CCP.
explanation: The CCP is buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer, so its positions offset. Market risk arises only conditionally, if a member defaults and the book is no longer matched.
originalText: The CCP has a matched book and bears no net market risk, but it takes on the counterparty risk of its clearing members, which is centralized in the CCP.

statement: A CCP eliminates counterparty risk from the market, because each trade is guaranteed and no party can default on the CCP.
explanation: Counterparty risk is centralized in the CCP, not eliminated. The CCP can still suffer losses if clearing members default.
originalText: The CCP eliminates counterparty risk from the market, because each trade is guaranteed and no party can default on the CCP.

statement: A CCP bears the net market risk of all cleared trades, because it is the buyer to the seller and the seller to the buyer.
explanation: Because the CCP takes both sides of every trade, its positions offset and it bears no net market risk.
originalText: The CCP bears the net market risk of all cleared trades, because it is the buyer to the seller and the seller to the buyer.

statement: A CCP has a matched book and bears no risk of any kind, even if a clearing member defaults, because its positions always offset.
explanation: If a clearing member defaults, the CCP no longer has a matched book and faces conditional market risk. It needs margin and default fund resources to cover possible losses.
originalText: The CCP has a matched book and bears no risk of any kind, even if a clearing member defaults, because its positions always offset.

statement: Under novation, the original bilateral contract is replaced by two new contracts in which the CCP becomes the buyer to the seller and the seller to the buyer, so the original parties no longer have obligations to each other.
explanation: Novation closes out the bilateral contract and substitutes the CCP as the legal counterparty to each side. Each party then faces only the CCP.
originalText: The original bilateral contract is replaced by two new contracts in which the CCP becomes the buyer to the seller and the seller to the buyer, so the original parties no longer have obligations to each other.

statement: Under novation, the original parties renegotiate the terms of their contract, with the CCP facilitating the process.
explanation: Novation is replacement of the contract, not renegotiation of its terms.
originalText: The original parties renegotiate the terms of their contract, with the CCP facilitating the process.

statement: Under novation, the original parties keep their mutual obligations and additionally agree to the CCP's terms.
explanation: The original mutual obligations are discharged by novation, not retained alongside the new contracts.
originalText: The original parties keep their mutual obligations and additionally agree to the CCP’s terms.

statement: Under novation, the CCP guarantees payment to the original parties but does not become a party to the contracts.
explanation: Under novation the CCP is itself the contractual counterparty to each side, not merely a guarantor.
originalText: The CCP guarantees payment to the original parties but does not become a party to the contracts.

statement: After a trade is novated to a CCP, the original swap remains in place between the two original parties and the CCP guarantees its performance.
explanation: Novation extinguishes the original contract and replaces it with two mirror-image contracts, each between one party and the CCP. A guarantee describes a different legal mechanism.
originalText: The original swap remains in place between Vintage Eagle and Vinyl, and the CCP guarantees its performance.

statement: Multilateral offset lets a CCP reduce counterparty exposure by centralizing trades that can offset each other.
explanation: Because novation puts the CCP between all members, offsetting claims across members net against each other, which shrinks total liabilities and exposures.
originalText: It lets a CCP reduce counterparty exposure by centralizing trades which can offset each other.

statement: Multilateral offset allows a CCP to increase the total notional value of trades without impacting the risk exposure.
explanation: Multilateral offset reduces exposure. It is not a way to add notional without adding risk.
originalText: It allows a CCP to increase the total notional value of trades without impacting the risk exposure.

statement: Multilateral offset provides a CCP with the leverage to negotiate better terms for each trade that it clears.
explanation: Offset is a risk-reduction effect, not bargaining power over trade terms.
originalText: It provides a CCP with the leverage to negotiate better terms for each trade that it clears.

statement: Multilateral offset allows a CCP to increase transparency and, thus, the predictability of market movements.
explanation: Transparency is a separate benefit of central clearing, and it does not make market movements predictable. Multilateral offset reduces counterparty exposure.
originalText: It allows a CCP to increase transparency and, thus, the predictability of market movements.

statement: Compression consolidates derivative contracts, reducing the number of contracts needed to maintain an equivalent position.
explanation: Compression cancels redundant, offsetting contracts and replaces them with fewer ones. Gross exposure and notional fall while net exposure is unchanged.
originalText: It consolidates derivative contracts, reducing the number of contracts needed to maintain an equivalent position.

statement: Compression allows financial institutions to expand their investment portfolios while maintaining net economic exposure.
explanation: Compression shrinks the gross size of a portfolio. It does not expand it.
originalText: It allows them to expand their investment portfolios while maintaining net economic exposure.

statement: Compression increases market liquidity by expanding the available derivatives that can be traded.
explanation: Compression reduces the number of outstanding contracts. It does not create additional tradable derivatives or liquidity.
originalText: It increases market liquidity by expanding the available derivatives that can be traded.

statement: Compression separates and categorizes derivatives based on their risk profiles for better risk management.
explanation: Categorizing contracts by risk profile is portfolio analytics. Compression cancels offsetting contracts.
originalText: It separates and categorizes derivatives based on their risk profiles for better risk management.

statement: Netting consolidates several transactions into a single net position, decreasing the number of settlements needed.
explanation: Netting combines offsetting claims into one net amount, cutting redundant transactions and settlements and hence credit exposure.
originalText: It consolidates several transactions into a singular net position, decreasing the number of settlements needed.

statement: Netting enables financial institutions to increase the number of outstanding trades without affecting risk exposure.
explanation: Netting reduces, not increases, the number of transactions that carry counterparty risk.
originalText: It enables them to increase the number of outstanding trades without affecting risk exposure.

statement: Netting increases the granularity of financial claims, providing more detailed information for risk assessment.
explanation: Netting aggregates claims into fewer, less granular positions.
originalText: It increases the granularity of financial claims, providing more detailed information for risk assessment.

statement: Netting allows institutions to avoid the CCP's centralized risk management system for more flexibility.
explanation: Netting is part of the CCP's risk management framework, not a way of avoiding it.
originalText: It allows institutions to avoid the CCP’s centralized risk management system for more flexibility.

statement: For derivatives that cannot be centrally cleared, multilateral compression can reduce notional exposure and simplify the portfolio in the bilateral OTC market without central clearing.
explanation: Compression cancels offsetting transactions and replaces them with fewer ones, even without a CCP. It reproduces part of the offset benefit of central clearing while preserving net exposure.
originalText: Use of multilateral compression to reduce notional exposure and simplify the portfolio without central clearing.

statement: A CCP requires initial margin from its clearing members to pre-fund potential default losses, sized to cover adverse price moves over an assumed close-out period at a high confidence level.
explanation: Initial margin is a buffer against future potential default losses, calibrated to price moves over the close-out period and a high confidence level, usually 99% or more.
originalText: To pre‑fund potential default losses, sized to cover adverse price moves over an assumed close‑out period at a high confidence level.

statement: A CCP requires initial margin from its clearing members in order to pay them interest on the excess cash they deposit.
explanation: Interest on excess collateral is a by-product of holding cash, not the reason margin is required. Margin pre-funds potential default losses.
originalText: To pay clearing members interest on the excess cash they deposit.

statement: A CCP requires initial margin from its clearing members to cover its operating costs, including technology and infrastructure.
explanation: Operating costs are funded by clearing fees, not by risk collateral. Initial margin pre-funds potential default losses.
originalText: To cover the CCP’s operating costs, including technology and infrastructure.

statement: A CCP requires initial margin from its clearing members to reduce the notional value of trades cleared at the CCP without changing members' risk exposure.
explanation: Reducing gross notional describes compression, a separate service. Margin does not reduce notional.
originalText: To reduce the notional value of trades cleared at the CCP without changing members’ risk exposure.

statement: The primary purpose of the variation margin a CCP collects is to reflect the daily mark-to-market profits and losses of open positions in cash flows between the CCP and its members.
explanation: Members whose positions lost value pay variation margin and members whose positions gained receive it. This keeps current exposure close to zero each day.
originalText: To reflect daily mark‑to‑market profits and losses of open positions in cash flows between the CCP and its members.

statement: The primary purpose of the variation margin a CCP collects is to pre-fund losses beyond a defaulting member's initial margin by mutualizing them across members.
explanation: Mutualizing losses beyond the defaulter's initial margin describes the default fund. Variation margin settles daily price changes.
originalText: To pre‑fund losses beyond a defaulting member’s initial margin by mutualizing them across members.

statement: The primary purpose of the variation margin a CCP collects is to guarantee a fixed final settlement price at contract maturity regardless of market movements.
explanation: Variation margin does not lock in a settlement price. It passes on price changes as they occur.
originalText: To guarantee a fixed final settlement price at contract maturity regardless of market movements.

statement: A CCP's default fund is a mutualized pool of member contributions used to absorb default losses that exceed the defaulting member's initial margin.
explanation: The defaulter's own margin is the first line of defense, and the default fund, to which all members contribute, absorbs losses beyond it.
originalText: It is a mutualized pool of member contributions used to absorb default losses that exceed the defaulting member’s initial margin.

statement: A CCP's default fund provides daily liquidity adjustments based on the marked-to-market value of members' portfolios.
explanation: Daily adjustments for marked-to-market changes are variation margin. The default fund absorbs losses beyond the defaulter's margin.
originalText: It provides daily liquidity adjustments based on the marked‑to‑market value of members’ portfolios.

statement: A CCP's default fund finances the CCP's investment in technology and infrastructure.
explanation: The default fund is loss-absorbing risk capital, not a development budget.
originalText: It finances the CCP’s investment in technology and infrastructure.

statement: A CCP's default fund pays members interest on excess cash posted as initial margin.
explanation: Interest on excess collateral is unrelated to the default fund. The default fund is a mutualized pool for absorbing default losses.
originalText: It pays members interest on excess cash posted as initial margin.

statement: Lengthening the assumed close-out period, because the cleared contracts have become less liquid, increases the initial margin a CCP requires on a member's portfolio.
explanation: A longer exposure period allows larger potential price moves, which widens the loss distribution and raises initial margin.
originalText: Lengthening the assumed close‑out period because the cleared contracts have become less liquid.

statement: Shortening the assumed close-out period increases the initial margin a CCP requires on a member's portfolio.
explanation: A shorter close-out period reduces potential price moves and so lowers initial margin.
originalText: Shortening the assumed close‑out period.
correction: Lengthening the assumed close-out period increases the initial margin a CCP requires on a member's portfolio.

statement: Lowering the required confidence level from 99% to 95% increases the initial margin a CCP requires on a member's portfolio.
explanation: A lower confidence level covers fewer scenarios and therefore lowers initial margin.
originalText: Lowering the required confidence level from 99% to 95%.
correction: Raising the required confidence level from 95% to 99% increases the initial margin a CCP requires on a member's portfolio.

statement: An upgrade of a clearing member's credit rating increases the initial margin a CCP requires on its portfolio.
explanation: Initial margin is driven by market risk and the close-out period, not by the member's credit quality, so a rating change does not raise it.
originalText: An upgrade of the clearing member’s credit rating.

statement: Wrong-way risk for a CCP arises when a clearing member's default makes the value of its cleared position fall sharply, so losses may exceed initial margin sized for normal conditions and the CCP should review the adequacy of initial margin and default fund contributions.
explanation: Wrong-way risk means exposure is largest when the member is most likely to default, so standard margin calibrations may be insufficient. Selling protection on an entity tied to the member's own health is the classic case.
originalText: The member’s default makes the value of its cleared position fall sharply at the time of default, so losses may exceed initial margin sized for normal conditions; the CCP should review the adequacy of initial margin and default fund contributions for such positions.

statement: Central clearing removes wrong-way risk because the CCP is the buyer to every seller, so no change to margin or default fund methodology is needed.
explanation: A CCP still bears member default risk and wrong-way risk, and complacency can leave margin undersized.
originalText: Central clearing removes WWR because the CCP is the buyer to every seller, so no change to margin or default fund methodology is needed.

statement: Wrong-way risk is a purely bilateral issue that is eliminated by multilateral netting of the member's positions, so a CCP only needs to monitor the member's credit rating.
explanation: Netting reduces exposure within a portfolio but does not remove the adverse correlation between default and position value. Monitoring ratings alone does not size margin for it.
originalText: WWR is a purely bilateral issue that is eliminated by multilateral netting of the member’s positions, so the CCP only needs to monitor the member’s credit rating.

statement: CCPs use macro-hedging to minimize exposure to major market risk factors and so reduce the market risk they face after a member default.
explanation: Macro-hedging with liquid transactions quickly removes most market risk from the defaulter's portfolio, limiting losses during liquidation and making the later auction more attractive.
originalText: Macro‑hedging to minimize exposure to major market risk factors and reduce the market risk faced by the CCP.

statement: After a clearing member defaults and its trades are not ported, a CCP first macro-hedges with liquid transactions and then auctions by sub-portfolio, because hedged portfolios carry little market risk and attract higher bids.
explanation: Hedging first neutralizes most market risk quickly, so each auction deals with low-risk sub-portfolios and risk falls to zero as each auction closes.
originalText: Pre‑default period, then macro‑hedging with liquid transactions, then auctions by sub‑portfolio, because hedged portfolios carry little market risk and attract higher bids.

statement: After a clearing member defaults, a CCP auctions the full portfolio and then macro-hedges the residual risk, because auction proceeds determine the hedge needed.
explanation: The order is reversed. Auctioning an unhedged book exposes the CCP and bidders to large market risk and would lower bids, so macro-hedging comes first.
originalText: Pre‑default period, then auction of the full portfolio, then macro‑hedging of residual risk, because auction proceeds determine the hedge needed.

statement: After a clearing member defaults, a CCP auctions first and uses macro-hedging only if the auction fails, because auctions remove all risk immediately.
explanation: Auctions are the last stage, and risk only reaches zero as each auction closes. Macro-hedging is the standard first step, not a fallback.
originalText: Auction first, with macro‑hedging used only if the auction fails, because auctions remove all risk immediately.

statement: CCPs accept only cash as variation margin.
explanation: Variation margin is effectively settlement of gains and losses, so it is normally paid in cash, whereas initial margin may also be highly liquid government securities.
originalText: Only cash is accepted as variation margin.

statement: Netting of variation margin across different currencies is possible at a CCP.
explanation: Netting works within a single currency only, so mixing currencies prevents netting for variation margin purposes.
originalText: Netting of variation margin across different currencies is possible.

statement: The primary source of CCP income is interest earned on assets held, rather than fees per trade.
explanation: Fees per trade are the direct source of CCP income. Interest on assets held is an indirect and secondary source.

statement: During the margin period of risk, most risk is eliminated by auctions in which the defaulting member's portfolio is sold off.
explanation: Macro-hedging, not auctions, removes most risk quickly. The auctions then bring the residual risk to zero.
originalText: During the margin period of risk (MPoR), most risk is eliminated by auctions in which the defaulting member’s portfolio is sold off.

statement: In a CCP's default management, the hedged portfolio is split into sub-portfolios and surviving clearing members submit two-way prices, with the best bidder winning each sub-portfolio, so that the defaulter's exposure is neutralised.
explanation: The auction is the step that transfers the defaulter's hedged sub-portfolios to surviving members through competitive bidding, closing out the CCP's exposure.
originalText: The CCP splits the hedged portfolio into sub‑portfolios, and surviving clearing members submit two‑way prices, with the best bidder winning each sub‑portfolio, so that the defaulter’s exposure is neutralised.

statement: In a CCP's default management, the CCP sells the entire unhedged portfolio to the single member offering the lowest fee, before any hedging takes place.
explanation: Hedging comes first, and the portfolio is auctioned in sub-portfolios to the best bidders, not as one unhedged block to a single member.
originalText: The CCP sells the entire unhedged portfolio to the single member offering the lowest fee, before any hedging takes place.

statement: The auction in a CCP's default management allocates the defaulter's unpaid losses across surviving members in proportion to their default fund contributions.
explanation: Allocating losses to survivors is loss mutualisation through the default fund. The auction is a trade-out mechanism for the defaulter's portfolio.
originalText: The CCP allocates the defaulter’s unpaid losses across surviving members in proportion to their default fund contributions.

statement: The auction in a CCP's default management transfers the defaulter's clients' positions and margin to pre-arranged backup members at pre-agreed prices.
explanation: Transferring client positions is porting, a separate action from the auction of the defaulter's own portfolio.
originalText: The CCP transfers the defaulter’s clients’ positions and margin to pre‑arranged backup members at pre‑agreed prices.

statement: Porting of a defaulted clearing member's client trades transfers the client positions, together with the associated margin, to a surviving clearing member that accepts them, preserving the clients' positions without liquidating them.
explanation: Porting is voluntary: the receiving member must accept both the portfolio and its margin, often as a pre-agreed backup member.
originalText: The client positions, together with the associated margin, are transferred to a surviving clearing member that accepts them, preserving the clients’ positions without liquidating them.

statement: Porting of a defaulted clearing member's client trades compels surviving clearing members to accept the client positions regardless of their own preferences.
explanation: Porting requires the surviving member to accept the portfolio and its margin, so it is voluntary rather than forced.
originalText: Surviving clearing members are compelled by the CCP to accept the client positions regardless of their own preferences.

statement: Porting of a defaulted clearing member's client trades means the CCP cancels the trades that are opposite to the defaulter's positions in order to restore a matched book.
explanation: Cancelling unmatched contracts describes tear-up. Porting transfers client positions rather than cancelling them.
originalText: The CCP cancels the trades that are opposite to the defaulter’s positions in order to restore a matched book.

statement: Porting of a defaulted clearing member's client trades splits the client positions into sub-portfolios and sells them to the surviving member submitting the best price.
explanation: Splitting into sub-portfolios and selling to the best bidder describes the auction of the defaulter's own portfolio, not porting of client positions.
originalText: The client positions are split into sub‑portfolios and sold to the surviving member submitting the best price.

statement: Variation margin gains haircutting is a CCP loss allocation method in which the CCP reduces the variation margin it pays to members whose positions have gained in value, while members who owe variation margin must still pay in full.
explanation: The shortfall is allocated to members with gains, who receive less than their full variation margin gain. Payers pay in full, so the CCP stays matched and funded.
originalText: The CCP reduces the variation margin it pays to members whose positions have gained in value, while members who owe variation margin must still pay in full.

statement: Variation margin gains haircutting is a loss allocation method in which the CCP reduces the initial margin of non-defaulting members to cover the shortfall left by the defaulter.
explanation: Haircutting initial margin is not part of this method. Only variation margin gains are haircut, and non-defaulting members' initial margin is not touched.
originalText: The CCP reduces the initial margin of non‑defaulting members to cover the shortfall left by the defaulter.

statement: Variation margin gains haircutting is a method in which the CCP applies a haircut to the value of securities posted as margin to reflect their price volatility.
explanation: A haircut on posted securities is a collateral valuation risk control. Variation margin gains haircutting allocates default losses to members with gains.
originalText: The CCP applies a haircut to the value of securities posted as margin to reflect their price volatility.

statement: Variation margin gains haircutting reduces the variation margin owed by all members, both those with gains and those with losses, by the same percentage.
explanation: Haircuts apply only to payouts to members with gains. Members who owe variation margin must pay in full, otherwise the CCP would be unfunded.
originalText: The CCP reduces the variation margin owed by all members, both those with gains and those with losses, by the same percentage.

statement: A CCP neutralises a defaulted member's market risk by macro-hedging the portfolio against major risk factors, auctioning the sub-portfolios to surviving members and, if the auction does not work, tearing up unmatched contracts.
explanation: Macro-hedging reduces the CCP's market risk first, the auction transfers the hedged sub-portfolios, and tear-up is the fallback to restore a matched book.
originalText: Macro‑hedge the portfolio against major risk factors, auction the sub‑portfolios to surviving members, and if the auction does not work, tear up unmatched contracts.

statement: A CCP neutralises a defaulted member's market risk by auctioning the entire portfolio as one block and, if no bids are received, haircutting the initial margin of non-defaulting members.
explanation: An unhedged single-block auction is inefficient, and haircutting non-defaulting members' initial margin is not an accepted fallback.
originalText: Auction the entire portfolio as one block; if no bids are received, haircut the initial margin of non‑defaulting members.

statement: A CCP neutralises a defaulted member's market risk by tearing up all contracts first, then macro-hedging, then auctioning the remaining positions.
explanation: Tear-up is a fallback after a failed auction, not a first step. The standard sequence is macro-hedge, then auction.
originalText: Tear up all contracts first, then macro‑hedge, then auction the remaining positions.

statement: In bilaterally cleared OTC derivative markets loss absorbency comes mainly from capital, with increasingly some initial margin, whereas in centrally cleared markets it comes mainly from initial margin and default fund contributions.
explanation: A dealer absorbs bilateral counterparty losses mostly with regulatory capital, while CCP members post full collateral including initial margin plus default fund contributions.
originalText: Bilateral: mainly capital (increasingly some initial margin); central clearing: mainly initial margin and default fund contributions.

statement: In bilaterally cleared OTC derivative markets loss absorbency comes mainly from initial margin and default fund contributions, whereas in centrally cleared markets it comes mainly from capital.
explanation: This reverses the two markets. Bilateral markets rely mainly on capital, and central clearing relies mainly on margin and default fund contributions.
originalText: Bilateral: mainly initial margin and default fund contributions; central clearing: mainly capital.

statement: In both bilaterally and centrally cleared OTC derivative markets, loss absorbency comes mainly from capital, because margin only covers current exposure.
explanation: CCPs collateralise with initial margin and default funds, which carry most of the loss-absorbency cost in central clearing.
originalText: Both markets: mainly capital, because margin only covers current exposure.

statement: Central clearing standardizes and mutualizes risk, which can help increase the liquidity of the underlying markets through greater predictability and confidence.
explanation: A CCP replaces many bilateral credit relationships with one standardized counterparty and common margin rules, so positions are easier to offset and close out.
originalText: Central clearing standardizes and mutualizes risk, which can help increase liquidity of the underlying markets through greater predictability and confidence.

statement: Bilateral clearing enhances market liquidity by allowing counterparties to negotiate credit terms tailored to their needs.
explanation: Bespoke credit terms fragment the market and hinder offsetting, so they do not enhance liquidity.

statement: Bilateral clearing inherently provides greater liquidity than central clearing because there are no standard margin requirements tying up capital.
explanation: Bilateral markets are not inherently more liquid, and tailored terms reduce the fungibility of positions.
originalText: Bilateral clearing inherently provides greater liquidity because there are no standard margin requirements tying up capital.

statement: Central clearing restricts market liquidity because the rigid CCP structure cannot adapt to market changes.
explanation: A CCP can improve liquidity through standardization and mutualization, rather than restrict it.
originalText: Central clearing restricts liquidity because the rigid CCP structure cannot adapt to market changes.

statement: A CCP gives a consolidated view of market exposures and can see aggregate risk concentrations, whereas bilateral clearing obscures them because it is decentralized.
explanation: In a bilateral market each pair of counterparties sees only its own trades. A CCP sits in the middle of all cleared trades and sees aggregate positions.

statement: Bilateral clearing promotes transparency because individual agreements let participants directly assess counterparty risk.
explanation: Bilateral parties see only their own relationships, so the market as a whole is opaque.

statement: Bilateral trades are customizable, so market risk assessments are clearer than the homogenized representations in central clearing.
explanation: Customization makes bilateral exposures harder, not easier, to aggregate and assess.

statement: In centrally cleared OTC derivative markets, only standardized, plain-vanilla, liquid products can be cleared, and participants are usually large dealers (clearing members) with others clearing through them.
explanation: A CCP needs standardized, liquid products so it can value and close out positions. Clearing members are usually large dealers, and other entities access the CCP through them.
originalText: Only standardized, plain‑vanilla, liquid products can be cleared, and participants are usually large dealers (clearing members) with others clearing through them.

statement: In centrally cleared OTC derivative markets, any product the two parties agree on can be cleared, and any market participant can become a clearing member.
explanation: This describes the bilateral market. Central clearing restricts both products and participants.
originalText: Any product the two parties agree on can be cleared, and any market participant can become a clearing member.

statement: In centrally cleared OTC derivative markets, only standardized products can be cleared, but any participant can join the CCP directly.
explanation: The product restriction is right, but access is through clearing members, which are usually large dealers.
originalText: Only standardized products can be cleared, but any participant can join the CCP directly.

statement: Complex, bespoke trades are cleared preferentially because CCPs are best able to manage non-standard risk.
explanation: Bespoke trades typically stay bilateral because they are not standard or liquid enough for a CCP to value and close out.
originalText: Complex, bespoke trades are cleared preferentially because CCPs are best able to manage non‑standard risk.

statement: Centrally cleared transactions offer greater transparency and operational efficiency than bilaterally cleared transactions.
explanation: Centralization gives visibility of aggregate exposures and streamlined netting and settlement.

statement: Bilaterally cleared transactions are subject to stricter regulatory oversight than centrally cleared transactions.
explanation: This is reversed. CCPs face heavier regulatory oversight than bilateral markets.

statement: Centrally cleared transactions typically involve higher counterparty risk than bilaterally cleared transactions.
explanation: This is reversed. CCP margining and loss mutualization generally lower counterparty risk.

statement: Bilaterally cleared transactions have standardized margin requirements, while centrally cleared transactions have negotiated margin requirements.
explanation: This is reversed. Bilateral margin is bespoke and negotiated, whereas CCP margin is standardized and enforced by the CCP.

statement: Centrally cleared markets offer more flexibility in contract selection than bilateral markets because of their collateral collecting process.
explanation: Central clearing trades flexibility for standardization. Only standardized, liquid products are cleared, with fixed, nonnegotiable collateral rules.
originalText: offer more flexibility in contract selection because of their collateral collecting process.

statement: Centrally cleared markets remain market neutral by netting trades.
explanation: Multilateral netting is a genuine benefit of central clearing relative to bilateral markets.
originalText: remain market neutral by netting trades.

statement: Centrally cleared markets formalize the default workout process by using a loss waterfall structure.
explanation: The loss waterfall is a formal, pre-defined default process, unlike an ad hoc bilateral workout.
originalText: formalize the default workout process by using a loss waterfall structure.

statement: Centrally cleared markets improve the counterparty risk picture by replacing the original counterparty with a series of counterparties.
explanation: The CCP and its members replace the original counterparty, which changes the counterparty risk picture and is cited as a feature of central clearing.
originalText: improve the counterparty risk picture by replacing the original counterparty with a series of counterparties.

statement: If a CCP lowers initial margin and correspondingly raises the size of the default fund, the cost of clearing falls but moral hazard rises, because a larger share of default losses is borne by other members rather than the defaulter.
explanation: Mutualized default fund resources are cheaper than fully funded initial margin. Less margin weakens the link between a member's behaviour and who pays for its default.
originalText: The cost of clearing falls, but moral hazard rises because a larger share of default losses is borne by other members rather than the defaulter.

statement: If a CCP lowers initial margin and correspondingly raises the size of the default fund, the cost of clearing rises, because mutualized default fund contributions must cover every member's default.
explanation: Mutualization lowers the cost of clearing compared with funding losses through larger initial margins.
originalText: The cost of clearing rises, because mutualized default fund contributions must cover every member’s default.

statement: If a CCP lowers initial margin and correspondingly raises the size of the default fund, both the cost of clearing and moral hazard fall, because losses are shared more widely among members.
explanation: The cost of clearing falls, but wider loss sharing weakens the defaulter-pays incentive, so moral hazard rises rather than falls.
originalText: Both the cost of clearing and moral hazard fall, because losses are shared more widely among members.

statement: A CCP's initial margin covers the defaulter's own losses in all but rare, extreme scenarios, and the mutualized default fund absorbs the extreme losses that exceed it.
explanation: Initial margin is member-specific and sized for about 99% confidence. Because a margin breach remains possible and tails are heavy, the default fund covers the excess.
originalText: Initial margin covers the defaulter’s own losses in all but rare, extreme scenarios; the mutualized default fund absorbs the extreme losses that exceed it.

statement: At a CCP, initial margin is pooled across all members, while the default fund is posted by the defaulter alone against its own portfolio.
explanation: The roles are reversed. Initial margin is the defaulter's own, and the default fund is the pooled, mutualized resource.
originalText: Initial margin is pooled across all members, while the default fund is posted by the defaulter alone against its own portfolio.

statement: At a CCP, the default fund absorbs the majority of ordinary losses, and initial margin is used only for small estimation errors.
explanation: The layering is reversed. Margin takes the first and most likely losses, and the default fund takes only the extreme tail.
originalText: The default fund absorbs the majority of ordinary losses, and initial margin is used only for small estimation errors.

statement: A 99% initial margin covers every possible loss from a clearing member's default, so a default fund is unnecessary.
explanation: A 99% margin still leaves a chance of a breach with potentially very large losses, which is exactly why a default fund exists.
originalText: A 99% initial margin covers every possible loss from a default, so a default fund is unnecessary.
